title: 1 Chronicles 27:1–15
context: The twelve monthly army divisions of twenty-four thousand each and their commanders. Many of these names also appear among David’s mighty men in 2 Samuel 23:8–39 and 1 Chronicles 11, with some differences in names and details that are noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: Now the children of Israel after their number, the heads of fathers’ households and the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and their officers who served the king in any matter of the divisions which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year—of every division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: The army divisions serve month by month, “of every division were twenty-four thousand.” Arminian readers see an orderly system that shared military duty fairly among the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David’s kingdom organized in an orderly way. The commanders in verses 2–15 correspond to names in 2 Samuel 23:8–39 and 1 Chronicles 11, with differences that are named rather than harmonized.

verses.text: Over the first division for the first month was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Jashobeam son of Zabdiel commands the first division. Arminian readers see a notable warrior given leadership, recalling his place in 1 Chronicles 11:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see experienced leaders appointed. Readers in this tradition note that the parallel lists differ in some details, and they do not attempt to harmonize them here.

verses.text: He was of the children of Perez, the chief of all the captains of the army for the first month.
verses.arminianNotes: Jashobeam is “of the children of Perez, the chief of all the captains of the army for the first month.” Arminian readers see his tribal lineage recorded alongside his role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the genealogical note connecting him with Judah through Perez. The verse highlights his prominence among the commanders.

verses.text: Over the division of the second month was Dodai the Ahohite and his division, and Mikloth the ruler; and in his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Dodai the Ahohite commands the second division, with Mikloth the ruler. Arminian readers note that Dodai may be linked with the father of Eleazar named in 2 Samuel 23:9, though the identification is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification tentatively. The mention of Mikloth adds an officer whose role is not explained further in the text.

verses.text: The third captain of the army for the third month was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah son of Jehoiada the chief priest commands the third division. Arminian readers see a renowned warrior entrusted with leadership, known from 2 Samuel 23:20–23.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Benaiah’s prominence. Readers in this tradition note that the description of Jehoiada as chief priest is recorded here without further explanation.

verses.text: This is that Benaiah who was the mighty man of the thirty and over the thirty. Of his division was Ammizabad his son.
verses.arminianNotes: “This is that Benaiah who was the mighty man of the thirty and over the thirty,” and his son Ammizabad is in his division. Arminian readers see past valor recognized in continued responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Benaiah’s earlier exploits remembered. The mention of Ammizabad suggests that responsibilities could pass within families.

verses.text: The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Asahel the brother of Joab commands the fourth division, “and Zebadiah his son after him.” Arminian readers recall that Asahel died in 2 Samuel 2:23, and note the phrase may indicate succession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the tension with Asahel’s early death. Some interpreters suggest the division bore his name or that the list reflects an earlier period, but the text does not explain it.

verses.text: The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Shamhuth the Izrahite commands the fifth division. Arminian readers note that he may correspond to a similar name in 2 Samuel 23 or 1 Chronicles 11, though the identification is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification cautiously. The repeated formula of twenty-four thousand per division shows the system’s regularity.

verses.text: The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite commands the sixth division. Arminian readers see another of David’s mighty men, named in 2 Samuel 23:26, given a monthly command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see faithful warriors entrusted with leadership. The list honors men whose earlier loyalty to David is recorded in the parallel accounts.

verses.text: The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Helez the Pelonite of Ephraim commands the seventh division. Arminian readers see leaders drawn from various tribes, reflecting the unity of David’s kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the inclusion of Ephraimites among the commanders. Helez appears in 2 Samuel 23:26, where his description differs slightly, a variation readers note without resolving.

verses.text: The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Sibbecai the Hushathite of the Zerahites commands the eighth division. Arminian readers recall his victory over a giant in 2 Samuel 21:18 and see courage rewarded with responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Sibbecai’s earlier service remembered. The tribal note links him with Judah through Zerah, showing the diversity of the commanders’ origins.

verses.text: The ninth captain for the ninth month was Abiezer the Anathothite, of the Benjamites. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Abiezer the Anathothite of Benjamin commands the ninth division. Arminian readers see Benjamites, Saul’s own tribe, serving loyally under David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the inclusion of Benjamin. Abiezer is named in 2 Samuel 23:27, and readers in this tradition value the evidence of tribal reconciliation under David.

verses.text: The tenth captain for the tenth month was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zerahites. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Maharai the Netophathite of the Zerahites commands the tenth division. Arminian readers see another of the mighty men listed in 2 Samuel 23:28 entrusted with a monthly command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity between the mighty men and the army divisions. The list keeps its focus on organization rather than individual exploits.

verses.text: The eleventh captain for the eleventh month was Benaiah the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah the Pirathonite of Ephraim commands the eleventh division. Arminian readers see a second Benaiah distinguished from the son of Jehoiada by his hometown and tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the distinction between the two Benaiahs. This Benaiah appears in 2 Samuel 23:30, and the careful identification prevents confusion between them.

verses.text: The twelfth captain for the twelfth month was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel. In his division were twenty-four thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel, commands the twelfth division. Arminian readers note that the name may correspond to Heleb or Heled in the parallel lists, though this is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the identification cautiously. With the twelfth division the military roster is complete, showing a year-round system of service.
